FROM CASUALTY PATTERNS TO A TEST PLATFORM

Which bike should we study?

Compare all makes, look inside the over-500cc group, and build a defensible shortlist for general motorcycle safety research.

COLLISION YEARS2020–2025

Great Britain · Riders and passengers
All motorcycle ages included

Casualty burden, not “most dangerous bike”. These are injuries to people riding the selected motorcycles. Mileage and fleet exposure are unavailable here. A high count does not prove that the motorcycle caused the injury or carries a higher risk per journey.

A PRACTICAL STARTING POINT

For one general-purpose research bike: start with a middleweight roadster

A Yamaha MT-07 with verified ABS is our provisional first candidate. It offers a roadster platform within the 501–750cc research group. This is an engineering judgement about the study platform, not a statistically proven optimum. A CBR650R is an alternative if sports-bike posture and controls are central to the study.

Manufacturer family information

Before choosing the actual machine: confirm the research question, rider fit, model year, brakes and electronics, service condition, instrumentation access and budget. STATS19 does not record ABS, cornering ABS or traction-control fitment. For learner/urban research, a 125cc platform may be a better fit; no single motorcycle represents the whole casualty population.

Bike type: a partial, curated view

Type is inferred from selected model-family labels, not supplied by STATS19. Unclassified records remain visible. Do not interpret the largest classified type as the largest type nationally. Sports and sports touring are combined because generic families span both.

How types are assigned

Manufacturer material supports broad family classifications. We intentionally leave ambiguous labels such as BMW R SERIES, BMW S 1000, HONDA CB and HONDA NC750 unclassified. Unclassified also includes models not yet reviewed; it does not mean “other bike type”. A current brochure is evidence for family style, not proof of historical variant or equipment. Cruiser, touring and retro coverage is limited to selected families. Off-road models and all other unreviewed families remain unclassified.

Model family × capacity band

Click a family to inspect its exact recorded capacities. Table shows the first 50 qualifying rows; export includes all.

Percentage rankings require at least 50 casualties per group. This limits very small denominators; it does not make the percentage a risk per journey. The minimum applies to table rows, not the totals.

Exact recorded displacement, not a verified variant. Missing displacement stays separate. A generic model label may combine multiple generations.

What supports this comparison?

Casualties are linked to their own vehicle using collision ID, year and vehicle reference. Only motorcycle riders and passengers are included. All six years reconcile to official national recorded motorcycle casualty, fatal and serious totals. No individual collision records are published here.

Recorded KSI combines fatal and recorded serious injuries. Severity recording changes affect comparisons across years. Adjusted estimates are available for 2021–2025 only: the retained 2020 extract uses older adjustment weights which do not reconcile to the latest national table. Selecting adjusted KSI moves the start year to 2021. The 2020 recorded counts do reconcile. Pandemic travel disruption affects comparisons involving 2020.

2020 comes from the retained 2020–2024 extract; 2021–2025 use annual files. Manufacturer is parsed from the recorded generic label. Labels are not fully harmonised across variants or spelling, so use family searches and inspect related rows. Missing models cannot reliably be allocated to makes or types.

Capacity, bike style, age of the rider, road environment and riding exposure are intertwined. These descriptive tables neither isolate a causal effect nor establish that training or equipment would have prevented an injury. KSI percentage is severity among casualties, not the chance that a rider will crash.
